title: OpenEP|NET
summary:
Background and study aims 
Cardiac arrhythmias (variations in the heartbeat) occur in about one-in-four people. They can impact broadly on quality
of life and dramatically increase health risks. The most frequent arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation. Atrial fibrillation
increases risks of health failure nearly five-fold, chronic kidney disease by 64%, coronary heart disease by 61% and
stroke 2.3-fold. Women have worse outcomes overall than men. Ventricular arrhythmias are the leading cause of
sudden cardiac death, responsible for 6 million annual fatalities.
Arrhythmias are often treated by procedures called Ablation or device implantation. Ablation is a specialised process
where small patches of tissue are destroyed under anaesthetic. Devices used for treating arrhythmias include
pacemakers (which keep the heart going at the right speed) and defibrillators (which reset the heartbeat if it goes
wrong). Ablation is an intricate and costly procedure which only provides an effective long-term solution in 50-80% of
patients, and we still don't fully understand its benefits.
During these treatments doctors collect an enormous amount of data. This includes details on the heart's structure
and its electrical activity triggering and regulating the heartbeat. This data is stored in various stand-alone formats
which makes it difficult to compare and analyse on a large scale. As a result, big data research has not progressed in
this field compared to other fields. To solve this problem our team developed a software tool named OpenEP. This
software can dramatically reduce the size of the collected heart data which makes it far simpler to analyse.
In this programme of research, we will use OpenEP, along with other tools, to make arrhythmia data accessible to
researchers. To ensure broad applications, we will link routinely collected data to important clinical outcomes, such as
heart attacks, strokes, or hospital admissions, and patient reported outcomes such as symptoms providing an end-to-end trace from data to outcomes.

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years or over undergoing electrophysiological assessment (electroanatomic mapping, cardiac implantable device recordings or ECG recordings)

What does the study involve? 
Patients will be able to opt out of the cohort and consent will be sought for inclusion when patients are approached to take part in future studies within the Programme. Once part of the cohort, patients who have consented may be approached to take part in other arrhythmia studies which will be added under this approval. These are smaller studies that focus on specific important health questions. These studies will either use data already collected or will require extra visits from participants.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Not provided at time of registration

Where is the study run from? 
University of Edinburgh (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
June 2026 to December 2029

Who is funding the study? 
Medical Research Council (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Steven Williams, steven.williams@ed.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Patients undergoing electrophysiological assessment (electroanatomic mapping, cardiac implantable device
recordings or ECG recordings)
2. Aged 18 years or over
Exclusion criteria:
1. Potential participant has registered their intention for their data not to be used for research, via the national-data optout (NHS England sites only)
2. Potential participant has registered their intention for their data not to be used for research, via direct communication
